Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to table copy of order in council P.C. 2432, passed June 20, 1946, further amending the wartime wages control order, P.C. 9384.
In connection with this amendment I wish to make the following statement:
Canada's anti-inflation programme, established in 1941, can, I think, be regarded as being something in the nature of an experiment. It can now be said that many economists did not think it would succeed and would break down because it ran contrary to the economic forces. However, for the most part it did succeed. In large measure that success was due to the unqualified acceptance of the programme by the people of Canada.
While it was a difficult enough task to put into motion the machinery needed to implement the anti-inflation programme, it is squally difficult to gear down that machinery and modify the programme. On previous occasions it has been stated in this house that the government's policy is to move out of the price control-wage stabilization field just as rapidly as it is considered expedient to do so. The current problem is one of timing the steps to be taken in decontrol.
In respect of wage stabilization, steps have already been taken to modify the wages order, ,and a further step is about to be taken. It is concerning this latest modification that I wish to speak in particular.
The important change proposed concerns section 20 of wartime wages control order 1943, P.C. 9384. That is the section which gives war labour boards the power to authorize or direct adjustments in wage rates.
The original clause (a) of subsection 1 of the section limited the board's powers to increase wage rates only to the extent necessary to rectify "a gross injustice or gross inequality". In January of this year that section was changed so as to enable boards to authorize or direct increases in any wage rates which were found to be low in comparison with wage rates generally prevailing in the locality. The amendment further empowered a war labour board to authorize an employer to increase wage rates on such other basis, and to such extent, as in the opinion of the board is reasonable in the circumstances and con-

sistent with the maintenance of existing prices of the goods and services which the employer sells.
While this amendment served its purpose during the period it has been in force, changing conditions during this transitional period have made it appear to us that the wage adjusting formula should be modified to permit war labour boards a wider discretion than they have had.
Under the present amendment, war labour boards may authorize or direct increases in wage rates if and to the extent that such boards find the proposed increases are "just and reasonable". The amendment cuts away from the over-all wage fixing formula some of the previously existing restrictive conditions. It places upon war labour boards a greater discretion-a discretion which, I am satisfied, will be fairly exercised by representatives of management and of the major branches of organized labour in Canada, who as members of those boards have had a vast amount of experience in administering this part of our anti-inflation programme.
Much has been said of Canada's contribution to the war effort. In my opinion this is not the time to review that contribution. This is the time to direct our thoughts to the present and the immediate future. The progress of Canada will depend largely on the process of reconverting the country from a wartime to a peace-time basis.
The next two or three years will be critical ones for the future economic development of Canada. If we fail to pursue sound economic policies during that time, damage will be done which will jeopardize our progress for years to come. I can tell you that the task of maintaining a reasonable degree of stability in our economic affairs at this time is much more complicated and calls for a much greater degree of judgment than was the case when we were fighting for our very existence.
Thanks to our policy of economic stabilization, which ultimately met with the active support of industry and of the great majority of organizations in the labour movement, we came through the war well. That has been true to date in this transition period. It is the responsibility of all Canadians, whether they be in the managerial group or the labour groups, to see to it that we do not have a repetition of the inflation that struck this country in the early twenties. We must not loss of sight of the fact that the forces which brought about the chaotic conditions of boom and slump after the last war are present in our economy now. An abandonment of control now would let loose forces which could

wreck the economic life of the country at a time when an orderly transition to peace-time conditions is a primary necessity, and the country would be worse off than if stabilization controls had never been imposed.
I have been in the labour movement long enough-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Wait a moment. Listen to what I have to say. I repeat that I have been in the labour movement long enough to know that the real target of labour is to raise the real standard of living.

What child did you bring
forth?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
It was not my hon. friend, I know.
I know that labour has, during these last six years, made greater gains in this direction than it has in any other like period in the history of the movement. The ideal should be to consolidate those gains. What I am afraid of-and I say this with all sincerity-is that any untoward advance in the present wage structure is going to do one of two things: either it will force prices up, whereupon the increased rates will count for naught, or it could force a buyers' strike to curtail production, and of course that will mean unemployment.
This government is in favour of good and fair wages; let no one think that any member of the government holds a contrary view. Good and fair wages are just that as long as they can maintain a real standard of living.
What all should strive for is production. A normal flow of goods and services will indeed form the real income of the community. It is the responsibility of management and labour, acting as a team, to work for the maximum production of goods and services, and anything which stands in the way of this is contrary to the best interests of all, particularly the wage earner.
What I have said has been for a definite purpose. I do not want anyone to think that, because the wartime wages control order has been amended, the lid is off. The revision of the order imposes upon all a very special duty, that duty being to work together through this transition period to the end that we can come out of it with an economy second to none. That should surely be a duty which all good Canadians should be glad to assume.
May I ask, Mr. Speaker, whether the minister's statement is debatable?

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: The statement made by the minister is not debatable.

Then I raise a question of privilege on behalf of the ordinary members of the house. I protest against the minister making certain statements which do nothing but eulogize the government, when it is not possible for other members to debate those statements. On a question of privilege I protest against it.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: The committee will remember that when I introduced this bill on May 28 I said that it was incidental to the resolution which was under debate until last Thursday night. Had I not been remiss in my duty on Wednesday last I should have announced that we would ask the house to take up second reading of this bill when the resolution was passed. It did pass the house shortly before eleven o'clock on Thursday night, and as I had not given notice that the second reading of this bill would be moved immediately afterwards I did not feel that I should do so, and I took the first opportunity then of informing the house that it would be called at this time.
In 1912 parliament passed several acts to extend northwards the boundaries of Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba. In the bill dealing with the extension northward of the boundaries of Quebec it was provided that the population of the added territory would not be counted in the population to be divided by sixty-five to find the unit of representation on redistribution of the membership of this house. In view of the fact that the population of Quebec is not now to be the determining factor to fix that representation it was felt that the restrictions which had been inserted in the legislation of 1912 should be removed. I pointed out that when the statute of 1912 was passed its coming into force had been made contingent upon concurrent legislation of the Quebec legislature, and that in fact concurrent legislation had been passed. It was only after it had been passed and the increase in area and the terms of that increase accepted by an act of the legislature of Quebec that the federal act was proclaimed.
Hon. members will note that it is proposed that this act shall not come into force until proclaimed, and shall not be proclaimed unless and until there is concurrent legislation of the

Quebec Boundaries Extension
legislature of Quebec. As a matter of fact, before it was introduced the government of Quebec was advised of its introduction, and that the proposal would contain the section that it would not come into force except on proclamation and would not be proclaimed unless and until the legislature of Quebec had concurred in amending the provisions of legislation which had originally been made with the concurrence of the legislature of the province.
At the present time the effect is nil. At the last census the population of the area was 3,067, and in the calculation would amount to less than one one-hundredth of one per cent of the total population of Canada; therefore it does not affect the unit of representation. If it is included it raises the unit of representation from 45,566 to 45,578; but a difference of twelve in the divisor has no effect at all when used in dividing the population of the other provinces. It is really incidental to the resolution adopted by this house on Thursday evening, and if passed and concurred in by the legislature of Quebec, and proclaimed, will leave the province of Quebec in exactly the same situation as all the other provinces of Canada. It will leave the statute of 1912, which concerned Quebec, with the same conditions as those originally placed in the statute extending the boundaries of Ontario and the statute extending the boundaries of Manitoba.

speechtext: Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services) moved the second reading of bill No. 56, to amend the Naval Service Act, 1944.
Is the minister going to make a statement?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Perhaps I had better say a brief word in explanation. The purpose of the bill is to amend the Naval Service Act by adding two sections, 2SA and 28B, in order to provide permanent authority for the formation, training and administration of the Royal Canadian Sea Cadet Corps. That authority exists at present by virtue of P.C. 3655 of May 26, 1941, an order in council passed under authority of the War Measures Act and continued in effect under the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945. As the powers conferred by that act in due course lapse, it is necessary to provide permanent authority under the Naval Service Act. The bill is similar to sections 59 to 62 of the Militia Act, which make provision for military cadets.
The Canadian sea cadet movement is by no means new. Since 1896, members of the Navy League of Canada have contributed, without remuneration, a large part of their spare time to the sea cadet corps. The primary object of the movement was not, I think it is fair to say, to train cadets for service during war time, but rather to help direct boys and young men along the road to better citizenship.
At the outbreak of war in 1939, the Canadian navy consisted, as hon. members are aware, of approximately 1,700 officers and men. One of the lessons we learned in the course of the growth of the navy to its war-time
[Mr. MacNicol.l
peak of over 100,000 officers and men was the value, in time of war, of the training that had been given to the sea cadet corps. True, cadets were by no means finished seamen, but they had in the course of their training absorbed many of the fundamentals of service at sea, and also the basic features of naval discipline. The value of this training was demonstrated in every theatre of operations in which the Canadian navy was engaged. At least 6,000 cadets passed from sea cadet corps to active service during the war, and among their numbers the navy is proud to count some of its most distinguished officers and men.
It was in 1941 that the naval service first took an official part in the affairs of the sea cadets. Since then the movement has been the combined effort of the navy league and the naval service. The navy league provides the corps with training quarters and at least one summer camp in each province. The general administration of the corps is attended to by local branches and committees of the league. Interested citizens act as sea cadet officers and they, with the committees, organize public support for the corps. The naval service supervises the training of the sea cadet officers and cadets, operates the summer camps, and lends the necessary training equipment. It is intended to continue this, arrangement, which has worked out most, satisfactorily.
In 1942 His Majesty the King, at the request of the government of Canada, was pleased to permit the sea cadets of Canada to use the term "Royal" as a prefix to their-name, so that the official name then became "The Royal Canadian Sea Cadet Corps."
During the war considerable emphasis was-naturally placed upon the value of the corps as a means of training youths for eventual active service with the navy. Now that the war is over, emphasis is again placed upon the primary peace-time object of the corps which, as I have said, is to assist in the development of good Canadian citizens. Yet always-in the background is the thought that should Canada again be faced with a national emergency, the training these youth are-receiving to-day will stand the nation in good, stead.
There are at present nearly 13,000 sea cadets, attached to approximately 100 separate corps located in all of the larger cities-of Canada, as well as in many smaller cities and towns. It is proposed to increase the-number of cadets to 15,000. The widespread national enthusiasm for the movement that is constantly being demonstrated makes it plain that that number could, without diffi-

Naval Service-Sea Cadets
culty, be greatly exceeded. However, for the time being at least, the funds and administrative facilities that are available make it impracticable to aim at a membership of more than 15,000.
Hon. members who have, as I have had, a son in the sea cadet corps, or who have become familiar by other means with the activities of the corps, will not need to be told of the fine work that is being done in building character and in keeping the boys interested in worth-while things during their leisure time. I have been informed by officials of the Navy League of Canada that there is no record of a single serious offence having been committed in Canada by a member of the sea cadet corps. I am not in a position to verify that statement, but I am quite prepared to believe that it is correct. This record may in some measure be attributable to the fact that the Royal Canadian Sea Cadet Corps attracts a good type of young boy, but I am quite sure that the training the boys receive and the spirit that prevails in the corps has had a great deal to do with it.
I trust the house will support the amendment to the Naval Service Act which will permit this corps to become a permanent part of our naval service.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy indeed to support this bill. I have been a member of the Navy League of Canada, Ontario division, for the last thirty years, ever since 1917, and for a number of years have been one of the honorary presidents. In that time I have been associated with a multitude of distinguished men and women across Canada who, as the minister has so kindly pointed out, have given their services freely. They have given, too, of their time and their means to build up this great organization.
I thank the minister for the encomiums he has paid the navy league for the achievements of the young men belonging to that organization. I was amused a few days ago when I received from Toronto a pamphlet in whieh appeared the definition of a sea cadet boy. Perhaps the minister has read it, but I think it would be worth while to put it on Hansard. This article was prepared by the Rev. E. M. Skillen, co-padre of "Admiral Mountbatten" Navy League Sea Cadet Corps. Happily the sea cadets name their corps for admirals or ships. I have forgotten the name of the Toronto corps. The article states:
A sea cadet is a boy. A boy was once classically defined as a "darling" at the age of two, a "nuisance" at the age of 8, at 18 "interesting," at 22 "a meal ticket," and at 25 married "and to blame for everything." The definition is
humorous but superficial, for it leaves out of account the straddling age of 12 to 16, the most important time in a boy's life.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The top limit is 19 years. It ranges from 12 to 19.

The minister referred to training. The Rev. Mr. Skillen makes reference to that feature, in these words:
First the boy is dressed in the finest uniform in the world, a uniform steeped in tradition and honour, and he is taught to respect the uniform and what it stands for. It teaches him the first lesson of good citizenship, faithfulness to ideals.
Those are some of the reasons why in 1917 I became interested in this movement. That was about the time the late Lord Jellicoe, the victor at Jutland, came to Canada. He and those associated with him gave the movement a tremendous impetus.
As the minister has said, the corps have grown in number to almost a hundred. I believe the exact number stands at 91, and they are found in the principal cities and towns throughout Canada. The objective in membership is 15,000. I am happy to say that during the war more than 10,000 of those trained in sea cadet corps in Canada entered the Canadian navy. This number would be almost 75 per cent of the number belonging to the corps. Then, about 14 per cent joined the army, and about three per cent the air force.
But the effect on total enlistments throughout Canada in all the services, through the work of the navy league since 1917 was much greater than can be shown in the percentages I have given. Years ago, when I had more time, I visited the corps all across Canada. One expects to find the spirit of the sea prevailing in the towns and cities along our coasts, but it has always been a revelation to me to witness the ardour and enthusiasm of the sea cadets corps at inland points. I have in mind the city of Winnipeg which at that time, if not to-day, had the largest sea cadet corps in Canada. It is a large corps. Regina also had a high class corps, as well as Calgary and Edmonton.
The training that these boys had received down through the years showed results during the war. The young men of the prairies were far removed from the sea, but they were encouraged to enlist for naval and sea work. They excelled and distinguished thmselves beyond anything that anyone would have dreamed possible on the part of boys who had never seen ships and who had never had anything to do with the sea. With the minister I rejoice in the marvellous work accomplished by the navy league down through the years.
Naval Service-Sea Cadets

I cannot speak too highly of the navy league. Every time it was mentioned in the house, particularly during the war, many hon. members have been ready to laud its achievements. I cannot close without mentioning a few of the outstanding Ontario men and women who have taken part in this work. I am sorry I have not the names of those in other parts of Canada, but perhaps other hon. members can mention them.
Those in Ontario include the patron, His Honour the Lieutenant Governor Albert Matthews. The dominion president is Mr. D. H. Gibson, C.B.E., a retired executive of the great Robert Simpson Company. He has carried into the administration of the affairs of the navy league the same careful business administration he exercised when building up that great company. The Ontario president is Mr. Gordon C. Leitch, another outstanding business man of the city of Toronto, who devotes his whole time to the administration of the Ontario division of the navy league. I believe last year he was able to raise close to $400,000 to carry on naval work, which was to the credit not only of the Ontario division but of the whole navy league. The secretary is Mr. Victor R. Ramsay. Among the honorary presidents are Lady Eaton, Lady Kemp, Mrs. A. E. Kirkpatrick, Mrs. R. C. Matthews, and among the vice presidents are Colonel A. E. Kirkpatrick, K.C., Mr. J. C. M. MacBeth, K.C., and a long list of others.
I rise with a great deal of pleasure to support this bill. Let me close by quoting the promise made by the sea cadet. This reads:
I solemnly promise to live up to the motto of the Royal Canadian Sea Cadet Corps for God, for King and for the empire, and further promise, as far as I am able, never to allow any one to do or say anything against my king or country.
I gladly second what the minister has said about the official figures showing that the sea cadets are never in trouble, that they are always an example to others. I have never heard of one of them being in the courts for a misdemeanor. The training is such as to make them real men in character, in deportment, in civility and in recognition of authority. Although their pledge does not call upon them to serve, they have shown that they are ready to serve.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to delay this bill, nor shall I repeat the many fine things that have been said about the Navy League of Canada and the sea cadet corps in Canada. Naturally I agree with everything that has been said. I commend the interest that the minister and his department have taken in this work during

the past several years. I rose simply to draw one matter to the attention of the minister. I suggest that the remuneration given to the sea cadet officers be in the form of a clothing allowance. In the past this has always been to compensate for out of pocket expenses, which may amount to a considerable sum at the end of the year.
I have in mind one chap who attended the sea cadet officers course at Cornwallis for two weeks last month. He then went to camp with the boys at Gananoque. At the end of the year he found that the amounts he received for expenses put him in a higher category and the result was he was being penalized by our own revenue department. I feel that this matter should be taken into consideration and these payments made in the form of a clothing or expense allowance.
Mr. NORMAN J. M. LOCKHART (Lincoln) : Mr. Speaker, I support what the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Lennard) has said. In my fair city there is one of the outstanding branches of the sea cadet corps. Many persons in that city have given of their substance as well as of their time to support this work, and they are finding considerable difficulty in getting new personnel to continue it. Every possible consideration should be given to continuing the interest which these young men have in this work. They have grown up over a period of eight or ten years and have now reached the point where they would be very useful to the organization, but, they hesitate to continue with the work because of financial considerations, although they have every other qualification. I feel sure the minister will give this aspect of the matter every consideration.

Mr. Speaker, the Social Credit movement will be behind the proposals made by the minister in this bill. We urge that the minister be ambitious in preparing our people for an emergency. He should not be apologetic; he should tell the people that they are in grave danger of having to face another struggle at any time. It is wisdom to be prepared. We should emphasize the aspects of this movement which involve health, training, and 'character development, and we must be more prepared in many of these things than we were in the last generation. People get the idea that all they are doing this thing for is character development. The Social Credit movement will support the minister in an ambitious programme.

The first question I want to direct to the minister

Naval Service-Sea Cadets
is whether his remark about including those of nineteen years of age is correct, because I understand from the bill that it does not include those of nineteen years of age. The second point is with regard to rates of pay, accommodation and medical care, and so forth, being left entirely to orders in council. I believe that on previous occasions there have been complaints of discrimination between the various arms of the service with regard to the cadet corps, that the naval cadet corps was not receiving the same pay as cadets in the army and the air force. Are these provisions to be made uniform, or is there to continue to be discrimination in rates of pay?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We are not in committee, but if no hon. member desires to speak I can deal with the matters which have just been raised by the hon. member for Yorkton.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: If no other hon. members wish to speak, the minister wTill now close the debate.

As the boys' sea cadet camp known as Rotary Island is located within almost a stone's throw of where I live, I should like to say just a few words. I have had the opportunity of visiting this camp on many occasions, and my impression is that good training supervision is the secret of the success of this organization. I believe that in most cases the instructors and trainers are good, and therefore I am heartily in accord with any advancement of this enterprise. It is a great work. I have a couple of questions to ask, but possibly I can do that in committee.

I just want to compliment the minister for bringing down this measure, and would like to suggest to him-I., am sure he has taken it into consideration-that the good will and the cooperation of the provincial departments of education be obtained in order that this whole movement may be successful.

I have in my riding two of the finest sea cadet corps in the country, one sponsored by the Kiwanis, and one at the Grove school. The Grove school is, I believe, one of the oldest sea cadet corps in Canada. Three hundred of its members went into the services in this war and the previous war. But since the war is over the members of the Kiwanis club of Peterborough-of which I am a member-have told me it is difficult to keep up interest in the movement, to bring the boys together. I suggest to the minister that he do everything possible to get boats and other
equipment for the boys in connection with their training. They need it, and it is one way of keeping the corps together.

speakeroldname: Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I will close the debate, if I may, by thanking hon. gentlemen who have spoken for their kind words about the sea cadet corps and the Navy League of Canada-all of which, of course, I heartily endorse. I did not feel that this was a bill which would provoke controversy, and I am glad that it is receiving such general support on the part of hon. members.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1 - Royal Canadian Sea Cadet Corps.

Has any arrangement been made that the ships' bells off the different corvettes, Fairmiles, and so forth, be sent to the cities and towns to which they belong? If the ship's bell of, say, the corvette Peterborough were sent to Peterborough, it would assist in the recruiting of sea cadets and1 help the morale of the boys.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am not quite sure. I
believe that where possible, and where the request has been made, ships' bells have been sent to the cities and towns for which the corvettes have been named, but I am not in a position to say whether that is the general rule. I am inclined to think it is not. I will take a note of my hon. friend's suggestion, and when the estimates of the naval service department are before the house I can perhaps reply in greater detail.
The hon. member for Yorkton asked, I think, as to the age limit. The ages, as I said, are twelve to nineteen, but up to nineteen. Boys over nineteen years of age are not eligible as cadets. In other words they can serve up to the time they enter their nineteenth year.
How many training centres will there be in Canada, and where; and how long will the cadets train each year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: By training centres does my hon. friend mean cadet camps?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There are fourteen in all.
Distributed throughout the country?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Distributed throughout
Canada-one at least in every province.
Naval Service-Sea Cadets
Has my hon. friend the names of them?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Yes. I would be glad to put them on Hansard:
Pownal, ten miles from Charlottetown on Pownal bay.
In Nova Scotia negotiations are under way for a camp site and will be settled shortly.
Camp Brock, twenty-eight miles from Saint John, on the Saint John river.
William Ewing camp, which is near Choisy, outside Montreal.
Rotary island, Gananoque, Ontario.
Princess Alice and Queen Elizabeth, twelve miles from Midland on Minnicog and Beausoleil islands.
Kitchigami, five miles from Goderich on lake Huron.
Lake Eva, which is on Purdy island in Eva lake, near Kawene, Ontario.
Ruttan, which is near Kenora.
Shepley island, which is an island in the Saskatchewan river not far from Saskatoon.
Wabamum, which is thirty miles from Edmonton.
Chestermore, which is east of Calgary.
A camp in British Columbia on Gambier island, some fourteen miles northwest of Vancouver in Howe sound.
What will be the period of training?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am afraid I have not that information at the moment, but, judging from the experience of my own son, the camp operates during a period of two months in the summer, and the boys go for periods varying from two to four weeks.

The minister has drawn attention to the fact that, strictly speaking, a cadet ceases to be a cadet on his nineteenth birthday. Of course after that those who show aptitude and who so desire may perhaps be granted commissions; they are extremely useful in carrying on the work of the corps, and even as instructors they are on occasion continued in the work of-the corps and give very beneficial service. The great impetus which came to the sea cadet movement at the beginning of the recent war was largely due, I think, to the interest which the minister's predecessor took in this movement. Before that, in the years between the wars and particularly as a result of the years of depression, grave difficulties were encountered by those who were endeavouring to carry on the work of the sea cadet corps. A great deal of the load fell on the shoulders of those in our communities who were sufficiently interested in the work, and sufficiently appreciative of the fact that such training was of the greatest value not only to the boy himself but to the neighbourhood, to ensure that the movement was carried on. In 1941 the sea cadet corps
TMr. Abbott.]
regulations were brought out. I understand that those regulations have been amended and a new set have been prepared but not issued. I shall be glad if the minister will explain the position with regard to the new regulations. Possibly he has been waiting until this bill should become an act, but there are quite considerable modifications, I am told, in the new set, and I should like to hear when we shall have them.
In the second part of section 1 reference
is made to the fact that the members and instructors shall be entitled to accommodation, medical care and pay and allowances, as may be prescribed. I should like to make this observation to the minister with regard to accommodation. In 1935 the government took over a school building in the town of Kelowna where there is a cadet corps which has existed now for a considerable number of years, a school building which was about to be demolished but which it was considered could be adapted to the use of an armouries. On that occasion I made a point of seeing to it that the sea cadet corps should have not only the use of the drill hall and of the miniature rifle range but also have a room and a storeroom. A sea cadet corps accumulates a very considerable quantity of government property, such as rifles, ammunition and various instruments used for training the boys, and prior to that time it had been very difficult to preserve these possessions of the government in the hands of the sea cadet corps. I then made arrangements that there should be two comparatively small rooms put at the disposal of the sea cadet corps, one for use as an office where the committee could meet, whose task it is to run the corps, and where the officer commanding and the petty officers could draw up their reports and fill up their forms, and next door to it a store roorfi which could be under lock and key, the window of which could be barred. And so the sea cadet corps was for the first time in its history with something which it could call its own in the way of premises.
There must be many other opportunities for the government to provide that minimum of accommodation which in my opinion is pretty nearly a necessity if an efficient corps is going to be ran. Prior to that time, that corps and another one in my neighbourhood went from pillar to post to get what premises were available at a cheap rate, and then they were turned out and had to find something else. I should like to hear from the minister something on that subject, and whether he will endeavour to see that in future, when

Naval Service-Sea Cadets
armoury buildings are being provided, the sea cadet corps of that neighbourhood have premises provided for them.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
First, as to the new regulations, these have not yet been issued; as my hon. friend has intimated, they are being held until this bill has been passed. They will be issued shortly thereafter. It may be a month or two, allowing for revision and printing, but he can be assured that they will be issued promptly. On the question of accommodation, I agree with what he has said, that in making plans for the construction of any new naval division buildings, if and when we are able to proceed with them, proper care be taken to see that facilities are available for the sea cadet corps.
When I visited the naval division in Saskatoon two or three months ago-it is a modern type of naval division, a building which was constructed during the war-I was pleased to find that adequate and suitable provision had been made therein for the local sea cadet corps. The estimates for this year contain an appropriation of something over $800,000 for the support of sea cadet work, and the committee can be assured that this work will be continued.

Can I take it from the
minister's remarks that in those centres where there is not an armoury or a national defence building or any sort, the government will look favourably on a sufficient grant of money to enable proper premises to be rented for the purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows,
the sea cadet movement is sponsored by the Navy League of Canada, and a substantial portion of the money which is used in its activities is raised by voluntary subscriptions. The government feel that it is extremely desirable that this should be continued because it enlists the support of public-spirited and representative citizens in different parts of the country and is not solely a government-directed movement. It is most desirable that this feature should be retained. I am not prepared to say that in districts where there is no naval division available, in which quarters can be furnished for a sea cadet corps, a specific grant could be made for that purpose, but I shall be happy to take my hon. friend's suggestion into consideration and bring it to the attention of the officers of the department to see whether something of the kind would be possible. After all, it is as broad as it is long. If the moneys raised locally do not have to be used for the rental of premises, they can be used for other purposes, and therefore the amounts made available through
government assistance can be used for some other purpose. However, I shall take the remarks of my hon. friend into consideration and see what can be done.

I warn the minister that I shall expect him to fight like a tiger when the new premises are being built, which are foretold of in the Okanagan valley. A new building is said to be in contemplation. By the way, it is the same minister, and I shall feel it all the more necessary to ask him to see to it that a sea cadet corps is properly provided for in the buildings which will probably be put up before many years are over in order to replace those that exist today. In my opinion it is essential, if the government is going to support this very worthy enterprise, that the necessary facilities be provided to enable them to carry on their work properly.

The corps in which I am most interested is housed at the moment in armouries under the direction of M.D. 2, and we are working harmoniously with the O.C. of the battery in charge of the armouries. Further to what the minister said about the sea cadet movement being under the direction of the Navy League of Canada and more or less on their own, I believe it remains that way to a great extent. I may add that both Hamilton and Burlington are considering the raising of considerable amounts of money- by private subscription, which is as it should be-for the erection of sea cadet headquarters in both places.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I feel it my duty to say that no one in Canada did more for the sea cadet corps than a former minister of national defence, the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling). It was one of his great works. When he was minister of defence and in opposition in other days he unfailingly supported the sea cadet corps.

Canada now has three
cadet corps, the sea cadets, the army cadets and the air force cadets. They all receive some, if not all, their financial assistance from the government of Canada. There are other boy organizations, such as the boy scouts, in Canada which in the past have, I believe, received government grants. It is highly desirable that there should be no duplication, in the expenditure of this money, and that there should not be undue rivalry between these various organizations-and by undue rivalry I mean attemps made by local scoutmasters or cadet leaders to get boys to transfer from one organization to another. In order that Canada's money may be spent as wisely
Naval Service-Sea Cadets

and judiciously as possible some coordination is required between the activities, training, terms of enlistment and so forth of these various cadet corps. Can the minister tell us whether any steps are being taken to coordinate the training activities of the three cadet corps? If so, is there any further coordination between the other boy movements of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
There is an inter-service
cadet committee in the three services. I am not able to say just how far that committee has progressed with coordinating the training in the three services. One thing that it does is to allocate corps on the basis of population, having due regard to the requests of local school boards and so forth, so that there will not be overlapping and duplication, particularly in smaller towns, as between the cadet corps of the three services. I think that is desirable. I do not believe very much headway has been made thus far in coordinating the training of the various corps. I do not know just how far that wjll be possible. My hon. friend could speak with greater authority on that than I can. I suppose the one purpose of the cadet corps, aside from its training value, lis to instil in the member of the corps a liking for and an interest in the particular service for which he is training, and so long as it balances out fairly well throughout the country on the law of averages I suppose we can leave to each service the determination of the type of training that may be given in a particular corps in the service. But I shall be glad to look into the matter a bit further. Perhaps when my general estimates are under review I can make a more complete statement in reply to the inquiry which my hon. friend has made.

In my own locality some men who are in the boy scout movement are members of the sea cadet committee and, it has never been my experience that there has been any conflict between the boy scouts and the sea cadet movement. I may not be right. Some hon. member said I was wrong. But so far as my knowledge goes there is complete cooperation. We do not take boys into the sea cadets until they are fourteen years of age, and at that time they are about ready to leave the boy scouts.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That coincides with my experience. In my own city Mr. R. C. Stevenson is extremely active in the boy scout movement and the sea cadet movement.

Is the inter-service cadet committee considering the standardization of pay and allowances, uniform conditions of service,

commissioning and so forth for the three cadet corps, or are they all handling their own organizations and directing them by different means?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There is an inter-service cadet committee in Ottawa and one in each military district as well; but on the point just raised by the hon. member I think that is a matter which is considered not by the interservice cadet committee but by the personnel members committee. I am not in a position to give a definite answer to that at the moment.
Is the government considering any national youth training or cadht movement which goes above and beyond a particular service?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not that I am aware of.
Has the government asked the inter-service committee to report on the feasibility of trying a national youth training movement?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I question whether that would be the function of this committee. The function of the committee is simply to correlate the activities of the cadet movement in the three services. I would think that is a matter of government policy which would hardly come within the purview of the interservice cadet committee.

There are only 15,000 sea cadets authorized, and the same number for the air cadets. That makes 30,000 young men in Canada to be taken up by these two services to be given training, which is an immense advantage. The remainder is left to the army. It seems to me that it would be well for the government to consider a scheme which would take in the whole of the country, to give youth all the benefits of the type of training which the cadet gets in these two services.

Are the sea cadets entitled to receive benefits from the Strathcona trust? I have attended various meetings of the trust committee in various provinces, but I have never seen any representative of the sea cadet service there.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot answer that question at the moment. I shall have to make inquiries and give my hon. friend the information when my estimates are under discussion.
Mr. GILLIS; The officers who organize and largely promote the sea cadets are obliged to purchase their own uniforms, are they not?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I believe that is correct.

Supply-Health and Welfare

Is any gratuity, allowance or remuneration given for the services of these officers? I had the privilege of attending two or three functions of the sea cadet corps in my own community, and I know that the officers who organized and promoted the cadet corps were hard workers. They were not men of means. Some of them were school teachers on a small salary. They have to dress well. I was given to understand that they have to purchase their uniform in addition to all the work they do, in promoting the organization. I thought it was unfair. The least the government should do would be to provide them with the uniform they have to wear, which is expensive.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We are now making provision for pay for the sea cadet officers, something which had not been provided for in the past; but no provision has been made for uniform allowance. The hon. member for Wentworth suggested that instead of paying the sea cadet officers we should give them such remuneration by way of uniform allowance, in order that it would not be taxable, and I said I would give that matter consideration. But as things stand at present there is a new provision in the regulations providing pay for sea cadet officers, and at the moment there is no provision for a uniform allowance.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I can tell my hon. friend, from my own experience in the days before the war, how generous Canada was in regard to allowances for uniforms. We had fifteen hundred air cadets in Vancouver with no uniforms at all. I was in defence at that time, and from the quartermaster's stores we obtained men's uniforms. The boys worked overtime for two nights, and we converted these men's uniforms into uniforms for the boys.

There has been a little confusion as to where the naval department stops and where the navy league steps in-in other words, as to where the line of separation should be drawn. The minister mentioned this in his introductory remarks. Equipment, supervision, training and so on I believe come under the navy league, but what about training grounds and matters of the kind? Are they for the navy league or for the governnment?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
In most centres the navy
league makes the premises available. In some centres where we have a naval division, suitable quarters are made available for the sea cadets, but probably it is fair to say that in most communities the premises are provided by the navy league through subscriptions raised from public-spirited citizens
who are anxious to support the movement. As I said earlier, personally I think this is a most desirable feature to be retained, because it gets people interested in the movement. You are always a bit more interested in something to which you have made a subscription, so I think it is desirable to retain it on that basis.

It was not too hard to get money for the navy league during the war, but it is a little more difficult to get it now. Some of these premises cost quite a bit to keep up. We have one in Peterborough which cost the Kiwanis Club over $3,000 to put in shape for the boys. The cost of maintenance is heavy, and I think the government should help out to some extent.

speechtext:
Section agreed to.

speechtext:
When the committee was last considering the estimates of this department on June 17, I tabled three sets of figures showing family allowance payments month by month, statistics based on the May payments, and further statistics based on family allowance payments broken down
Supply-Health and Welfare

-by provinces. These appear at page 2587 and following of Hansard. At that time, in response to some requests, I promised to make a brief statement about family allowance administration, in view of the fact that we have almost completed a year.
Hon. members will recall that the act came into force on August 15, 1944. The department which was to administer it, the Department of National Health and Welfare, came into existence on October 13, 1944, and under the terms of the act payments were to begin as from July 1, 1945. We have made payments now for twelve months. The twelfth payment, in respect of the month of June, 1946, has just been issued; but the statistics are not yet available in respect of that month. We hope they will be available next week. Generally speaking the records are kept in such a way that we can have a complete breakdown of the payments, province by province, about a week following the issue of the last cheque from the regional offices at the capitals of the provinces.
Hon. members will recall that in order to effect payment in the month of July, 1945, it was necessary to conduct a registration of all children in respect of whom parents wanted to receive payments. That registration was begun in Prince Edward Island in February,
1945,	and was carried on throughout the rest
of Canada beginning March 22, 1945. It is now possible to say that 92 per cent of the children under sixteen years of age are registered children in respect of whom payments are made under the act. The bureau of statistics estimates that there are 3,610,000 children in Canada under sixteen years of age, and in May, 1946, payments were made to 1,420,233 families in the amount of $19,934,614 in respect of 3,330,763 children. The average allowance per family was .$14.04 per month, and the average per child was $5.98 per month.	.
In regard to the size of families. 81-5 per cent had three or fewer children. In March,
1946,	one family was paid fc)r fifteen children; thirteen families for fourteen; 106 families for thirteen; 320 families for twelve; 1,132 families for eleven and 2,871 families for ten. Therefore some 4,443 families were paid family allowances on behalf of ten or more children. Families numbering four to nine children inclusive represent approximately 18-2 per cent of the total number of families in receipt of family allowances.
The hon. member for Eglinton last Monday asked me to produce a table to give a classification of families, by numbers of children, broken down by provinces. With the unanimous consent of the house I should like to place that table on Hansard. This gives the

I believe that hon. members generally are familiar with the administration. It would be surprising if they were not, owing to the fact that so many people in their respective constituencies receive family allowances. I must say that hon. members have been most considerate in dealing with regional offices and with the Ottawa departmental offices. The amount of correspondence we have received has been surprisingly small, when one considers the large number of families and children involved.
Administration has been carried on in nine regional offices situated . in the capital cities of each of the provinces. At each of the regional offices is a regional director and a staff connected with family allowance administration. In addition, and in the same building there are treasury officials. We have been exceedingly fortunate in having the closest possible cooperation between the family allowances staff which registers the births and conducts the greater part of the correspondence, and the treasury staff and officials of the comptroller of the treasury, who actually issue the cheques.
As at March 1,1946 there were in the family allowances regional offices a total of 489 employees who were either temporary or permanent; and in addition there were 492 employees who were employed on a casual or hourly rate basis. Those 492 were largely engaged in doing the work of verifying the backlog of registrations of births. Hon. members will appreciate that in the first year of administration we had a peak load in the registration of births, in that we had to conduct registrations of all children under sixteen, but we had approximately fifteen or sixteen times the task in a normal year. The work of verifying births has been largely completed.
As hon. members are aware, under our system applicants for family allowances are not required to furnish birth certificates. We make verifications in our offices in this fashion: We have made arrangements with each province under which the office of vital statistics in the province is furnished by us with Recordak equipment. sixteen years. The film is sent to Ottawa, where the information is put on Hollerith cards by the dominion bureau of statistics. Those cards are used to print automatically and in alphabetical order, arranged by years for each province, a register of the births and deaths of children under sixteen years in those provinces. Similar information is secured with regard to the children in the northwest territories and the Yukon, and also in connection with immigrant children.
In this way there has been built up a set of registers which, in the first instance, are kept in the family allowances offices. When an application is received, that application is checked against the register. There is written into the register the family registration number so as to prevent any double claim in respect of the same child.
The work of verification which I have just described is more than half completed. I am happy to say that thus far it has disclosed a very small number of cases of fraud. So far we have found only two cases in which there is a suspicion of fraud, in which the circumstances are such, as to warrant prosecution. That is an extraordinary tribute to the essential honesty of the parents of the children of Canada, when one thinks that with almost a million and a half registrations we have so far found only two cases which appear to show fraudulent registration. Those will be prosecuted through the usual channels. In addition, there has been a number of cases of forgery. About seventy-five claims have been made on the banks thus far, and I believe all those have been recovered.
The work of registration has been greatly simplified in Canada because the registration is so very simple in comparison with other government forms, and also in comparison with family allowance application forms used in other countries. We have found that it has worked well. An unusual feature of this administration is that we use only two printed forms, one of which is an application form and the other a supplementary application form. All other correspondence is conducted by ordinary letter. This, we find, has worked out well. It makes the administration more human; it prevents any delay owing to a lack of proper forms in the proper language at any point in Canada.
As hon. members may imagine, the correspondence is of considerable volume, and refers chiefly to changes in address, reporting deaths of children, or making inquiries as to amounts of payments. Actual letter correspondence totals about 133,000 letters a month. In addition, the family allowance administration makes changes automatically in the amount of

payment owing to changes in the size of a family or the age of children. There are in this way some 70,000 automatic changes each month. In addition, there are 31,000 changes of address.
Altogether this represents a substantial bulk of correspondence. The procedure for payment, after the form has been received applying for family allowance and payment is authorized, is carried out with, I believe, one of the most modern sets of business machinery ever to be assembled in Canada. Payments are made through Addressograph cheque-writing equipment. The cheques are issued on fairly stiff paper, which is punch-holed for automatic computation on International Business Machines equipment. In addition, in the larger offices there are envelope stuffers and other types of mechanical equipment which have enabled the administration to keep down the cost to a figure which we regard as reasonably good, in view of the fact that we have been operating for only a year, when the job of complete registration and verification of a backlog of sixteen years has not yet been completed.
When the bill was before the house on July 31, 1944, I was asked, as reported on page 6829 of Hansard, for an estimate of the cost of administration. Based upon the experience of administering dependents' allowances and other large scale payment operations in Canada, as well as the cost of administration of the children's endowment plan in Australia and the children's allowances in New Zealand, which were the best comparable costs, we arrived at a figure of from one per cent to two per cent, or from $2,000,000 to $4,000,000. I suggested that the figure of $2,000,000 was a target to aim at and that I thought it would be quite possible we would come within the figure of $4,000,000. Actually the cost of administration this year is higher than the $2,000,000 figure, but from the experience we have had so far we estimate that in a normal year, after the backlog is taken care of, the costs will amount to the following:
Department of National Health and Welfare, $1,850,000.
Department of Public Works for rentals, furniture and services, $80,000.
Treasury, $1,944,000.
The last item includes $636,000 a year for postage paid by the treasury on family allowance cheques. The total estimated expenditures is $3,874,000, which is 1-6 per cent of the estimated amount of the family allowances payable of $240,000,000. In other words, it comes within the figure we mentioned back in 1944 and we hope that this estimate will be improved upon.

Supply-Health and Welfare
With regard to the working out of family allowances generally, I think it is fair to say that from all the experience we have had the results have more than exceeded our expectations. While there are exceptions, as there must be in any large scale operation of this kind, the majority of parents spend the money for the health and welfare of their children. It is interesting to note that since family allowances were introduced in Canada in July, 1945, a bill has been passed through the British House of Commons providing for family allowances which will come into effect on August 6, 1946. By then we shall have family allowances in operation on relatively similar bases in New Zealand, from 1926; in Australia, from 1941; in Canada, from 1945 and in the United Kingdom, from 1946. In addition, family allowances on a smaller scale have been in operation in Eire since 1945.
Hon. members may be interested in knowing what the different payments are. They are familiar with the sliding scale arrangement in Canada whereby payments run from $5 to $8 per child, with a reduction in the case of children after the fourth. The average payment in Canada is $5.98 a month. In Great Britain the allowance is five shillings a week with respect to all children after the first, which, at the rate of exchange of $4.44 to the pound, works out to $1.11 a week. The total allowances a month amount to 21-7 shillings or $4.81 in Canadian funds. If we average that for all children in England for the purposes of making a rough comparison, we find that the amount per child a month is $2.11. In England they aim to put into effect by stages the provision of school lunches and milk for children, which will gradually build up into quite a sizable sum.
In Australia payment is made with respect to children after the first at the rate of 7-5 shillings a week which, at the rate of exchange of $3.55 per pound, works out to $1.33 a week. The monthly payments amount to 32-5 shillings, or $5.78 in Canadian funds. The average for the whole population gives a figure of $2.84 per child a month. Since the Canadian plan came into force the payments in New Zealand were increased and are now made in respect of all children. The allowance is 10 shillings which, at the rate of exchange of $3.55 a pound amounts to $1.78 in Canadian funds a week or $7.31 a month. It is difficult to arrive at an average for the whole population because the payments in New Zealand are not made in respect of all children. There is quite a high income test which along with other factors reduces the number of children from 100 per cent to something less
than that figure. It will be seen that the monthly rate of payment in New Zealand compares favourably with that in Canada as they have increased' the rates in New Zealand, since our legislation was passed.
The number of cases in Canada where we have found it necessary to divert the payment from the mother, or from the father in the absence of the mother, to some other parent or trustee for the child, has been found to be much smaller than was anticipated when the family allowance plan came into effect. We have had the close cooperation of provincial and other authorities with regard to the provision that payment will be made only in connection with children who attend school. In every part of Canada there has been a substantial increase in school attendance, which is one of the fortunate by-products of family allowance payments.
We receive a large number of unsolicited letters from parents telling us of the ways in which they spend the money. If hon. members are interested I can show ihem copies of this correspondence. These letters indicate a degree of cooperation and the recognition of the fundamental purposes of the family allowance provisions that is most moving. We hear from parents in different parts of Canada as to how they are spending the money for the welfare and health of their children. Many unusual cases are reported, many of them exceedingly moving. Altogether I think it is fair to say that, from the point of view of helping to provide for the health and welfare of children, and of enabling children to have a more equal chance in life irrespective of the size of their families, the place of their residence, or the income of their parents, family allowances have proved themselves to be a substantial contribution to that end we all have before us-of giving a better life to all Canadians.

I feel it my duty to say
a word at this time in support of the minister, his staff, and the way they have carried out this family allowance plan. I speak from considerable experience in saying that the money has been well spent. Children are better clothed; they have better food, and I suppose that once in a while they have better entertainment. It is a large amount of money which is spent on family allowances, but compared with the amount which was spent and wasted on war, the monetary reformers who used to be in this house- perhaps some of them are lingering around yet- .

Not "lingering".

iMr. MoIVOR: -would say that this money has been spent in the best possible way. Keep money in circulation and you will increase employment. . . ,	.
However, what I rose to do was to commend the minister and his staff, and you will notice that not all his experts belong to the male sex.
I have heard criticism levelled at Doctor Chisholm, and I think it has been overemphasized. When one considers that a deputy minister whose offices occupy only a small part of the Jackson building js held up before Canada as a menace; when one realizes that there are hundreds and thousands of ministers who twice a Sunday have their opportunity to tell mothers and fathers how to train their children in the way they should go, I think the statement of the deputy minister is being overestimated. I judge men as I find them, and I feel quite keen about this. I have had some experience with the deputy minister, and I have found no deputy more experienced or efficient than Doctor Chisholm. In one hour after I got a request from Fort William I interviewed the minister; I went to the deputy minister; I had the assurance that $200,000 would be made available for the care of Indians in the sanatorium at Fort William, and I was back in the hall where I started on my mission. If you do not call that efficiency I do not know what you would call efficiency. I do not agree with all Doctor Chisholm's views, but I do not think the minister would have the right to muzzle his deputy. All of us have our own ideas about things. I have mine, and my conviction is that the minister would be making a dastardly mistake if he got rid of his deputy minister.

But you were looking
for some money.

I pay a tribute to the
common sense of the minister in holding on to him.

What has been done to inform parents as to the best use that can be made of the family allowance? The minister has spoken of films and so on. I presume some of these have that end in view. Will he tell the committee what kind of advertising, and to what extent, these films display? If we are spending money on publicity, I suggest that the best possible kind of publicity is that which will encourage people to improve the nutrition of the family.
A second point I wish to raise is this. How is a check made to see the manner in which the money is being spent in the home? That is important. We should not try to regiment or over-inspect people, but I am often asked that question with regard to family allowances: How do you know that the money is being used for the purpose for which it was intended? I heard the minister say that a majority of mothers-and. by the way, it is a good thing that the payment is made to mothers-are spending the money on additional nutrition, clothing and so on for their families; but what check is being made in this regard and to what extent is this publicity directed toward the encouragement of people to improve nutrition?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
In answer to the first question as to the general objects of this publicity, it was quite obvious that we could not secure prompt and accurate registration without telling the people what family allowances are, where they could obtain registration forms, what they were expected to do and how they should fill out the forms, so that a large proportion of the total expenditures on publicity and information was devoted to that object. I 63260-175
think it paid off in results because, instead of having twenty or twenty-five per cent of subsequent correspondence as a result of improper registration, the total correspondence amounted to something like five per cent. Incidentally, the graphic sheet issued with the application form represented the first illustrated sheet of the kind used for that purpose. It suggested how government forms should be made out. We received only one complaint about the use of that form, which was published in a newspaper, and it undoubtedly secured effective results.
The second purpose of the publicity was to bring to people's attention the relation between income tax and family allowance. That was not a simple thing to explain or deal with, and a second series of advertisements were necessary in that regard. Their purpose continued after the month of June or July, 1945, and that was almost entirely- I believe entirely-directed to the objects mentioned by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, that is to say, bringing it home to mothers and other recipients of family allowances that the money was intended for the use of children, that it should be spent on food and certain types of clothing and other things which would contribute to the health and welfare of the children. In order to do that we had two films prepared and shown partly through the commercial theatres and partly through the non-commercial, nontheatrical circuits of the national film board, and through other agencies that usually show films. Hon. members all realize what a considerable proportion of the population is reached in that way. What is perhaps more important than anything else, we inserted in each of three family allowance envelopes a graphic sheet, so that the mother, on opening the envelope and receiving the cheque, would also receive a sheet giving in graphic form suggestions as to how payments should be used so as to inure to the welfare of the child. I think it has received a favourable response. We could think of no better way of bringing it home to the families of practically all the children of Canada-as I say, of 92 per cent of the children of Canada; and we propose to issue these staffers in one form or another about three months apart, not more often, because if they went out more often than that people would get accustomed to them and they would find their way more speedily into the wastepaper basket. On opening the cheque, they see one of these graphic sheets, it takes only a minute or less to see the whole thing, to take it in, and some part of the suggestion will remain.
Some nutritional surveys are being conducted among children, are they not?

First of all, I wish to compliment the minister. Since I have been a member he is the first minister to recognize officially that all the efficiency and all the devotion are not confined to the male of the species within his department.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: That is not correct. May I point out to the hon. member-and I do this with great reluctance because of my great friendship for the Minister of National Health and Welfare-that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is not the first minister to recognize the female of the species. The Minister of Labour did that two years ago when he brought in Mrs. Eaton.

May I point out to the Secretary of State that I said, "since I have been a member", which dates from last June.
I wish to compliment the minister on the administration of his department, and I have only two or three suggestions to make. Here we have quite a substantial investment in the youth of our country, and I think it is the best investment, the best expenditure, the government makes in the course of the year. We are now investing $250,000,000 in the children, who will be the backbone of the nation. I consider it important and useful to establish family allowances to take care of that particular group because, when I consult the figures on infant mortality-and I think this is a startling comparison-I find that in the five years from 1940 to 1944 more than three times as many babies died in Canada, where there was no war, as Canadian soldiers died in overseas service. The figure given by the infant and maternal welfare branch for infant deaths in the first year of life was 130,095 during that five-year period, while
the casualties of the army, navy and air force numbered 40,861. So one can see the terrific loss of lives in the first year of life, and the great need to do something to save the lives of our children. If we are to invest $250,000,000 in children up to sixteen years of age, we should go back even farther than the birth of the child and extend care during the prenatal period so that children would have the best possible chance of surviving the first year of life.
I find, too, that there is a great difference in the chances of survival as between the various provinces. In British Columbia, for instance, the mortality rate is 35 per 1,000 live births; they have the best record. That figure varies up to a rate of 77 deaths per
1,000	live births in New Brunswick. Here I must ask for some latitude and the indulgence of the minister if my remarks extend somewhat far afield. At the moment I am slightly out of order, but I want to point out that this is significant, because it proves that 77 can be reduced to 35, and it shows that it is possible to save the lives of more than half those babies who now die in the first year of life. That is the most valuable aspect of this report.
There is another report, coming from the same department, which indicates that we have reduced our maternal death rate from 10-1 in 1935 to 5-6 in 1943. I think everyone will agree that one mother dying and leaving a home broken and bereaved is a tragedy, but that the more than 800 mothers who died in one year according to the most recent survey constitute a very great tragedy indeed; and our statistics prove that more than half those mothers could have been saved if they had been given proper medical attention. So I would say to the minister that while this is a valuable step we have taken, we must protect this investment by extending our operations a little farther to take in not only the first sixteen years but also the prenatal care of the mother. We must make sure also that there is the proper publicity, the proper educational agencies maintained, so that mothers will know how to care for their children and for themselves.
I want to make just one suggestion in regard to this expenditure. I wish the period covered could be extended from sixteen to eighteen years in the cases of children taking secondary education. I speak from experience, because for the last three years my child has had to live away from home. I was able to collect the family allowance only for the matter of a few months. My child is beginning university this fall and becoming very expensive, and I have no family allowance. I shall be able to look after her, but I am thinking

So I wish the period could be extended to eighteen years to- .cover children who are trying to get an education.
